title: Ṛtaṃ tapaḥ: what austerity is
theme: A list of virtues and rites, each called austerity, ending with meditation on Brahman as the austerity.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «ऋतं मनसा यथार्थवस्तुचिन्तनम्» — thinking things as they are
Sāyaṇa: «सत्यं वाचा यथार्थभाषणम्» — speaking as things are
Sāyaṇa: hearing the two Mīmāṃsās, on the meaning of the earlier and later Veda
Sāyaṇa: «शान्तं शान्तिर्बाह्येन्द्रिया- भ्यन्तरेन्द्रियोपरतिः» — the outer and inner senses at rest
Sāyaṇa: «दानं धनेषु स्वत्वनिवृत्तिः परस्वत्वापादनपर्यन्ता» — giving up ownership of wealth so far as to make it another’s

words.gram: n. nom. sg. (as printed; m. yajñaḥ elsewhere)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «यज्ञो-ऽग्निहोत्रादिः» — the agnihotra and the rest

words.role: with the next two, qualifies brahma

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «भूरादिलोकत्रयात्मकं विराहरूपं यद्ब्रह्मास्ति» — Brahman in the form of Virāj, which is the three worlds
Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara gloss the imperative: «एतद्ब्रह्मोपास्स्व» (Sāyaṇa) — meditate on this Brahman

sandhi.type: m before a consonant; visarga before s
sandhi.rule: ṛtam becomes ṛtaṃ before t; tapaḥ before s is written tapas s (Taittirīya doubling).
A visarga becomes s before t.

sandhi.type: suvaḥ before b; a + e; t before a vowel; a + e; t before t
sandhi.rule: suvar brahma; brahma + etat → brahmaitat (a + e = ai); etad upāsya (t → d before a vowel); upāsya + etat → upāsyaitat; etat tapaḥ.

morphology.note: The base reads upāsya, the gerundive ‘to be meditated on’ (or a gerund, ‘having meditated’); the Tirupati e-text, in a second copy of the anuvāka it prints, has उपास्व, and both Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara gloss the imperative upāssva, ‘meditate!’. The meaning is close; the base is kept.
The base writes the double tt (सत्त्यं); the other witnesses have सत्यं. The word is satyam.
Neuter in form here, matching the neuter nouns of the list; yajña is usually masculine.

translation.literal: Right is austerity; truth is austerity; learning is austerity; calm is austerity; restraint is austerity; tranquillity is austerity; giving is austerity; sacrifice is austerity. Earth, mid-air, heaven: this Brahman is to be meditated on — this is austerity.
translation.readable: True thought is austerity; true speech, learning, calm, self-restraint, quiet of mind, giving and sacrifice are each austerity. But to meditate on Brahman, which is earth, mid-air and heaven, that is austerity.

syntax: Eight equations of the form X tapaḥ (‘X is austerity’), then the vyāhṛtis with brahma etad upāsya and a final equation, etat tapaḥ, which the commentators read as the climax.

ambiguities.note: The base’s upāsya can be a gerundive (‘is to be meditated on’) or a gerund (‘having meditated’); the commentators gloss the imperative upāssva. The final etat tapaḥ then means ‘this meditation is the austerity’.

ambiguities.topic: how the list relates to the end
ambiguities.note: Sāyaṇa ranks the first eight as lesser austerity and the meditation as the highest («तदेतत्सर्वमर्वाचीनं तपः» and «तदेतदुपासनमुत्तमं तपः»); Bhāskara makes them its limbs («ऋतादीनि त्वस्याङ्गतया कुरु»). The text only lists them side by side.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose list, one printed line of 46 syllables; no metre is claimed.

beginner: A list that redefines a word. Tapas usually means harsh discipline or self-denial. Here eight ordinary goods are each called tapas: true thinking, true speaking, learning, calm, self-restraint, quiet of mind, giving and sacrifice. Then the list turns: Brahman, which is earth, the space between and heaven, is to be meditated on, and that meditation is tapas. Sāyaṇa explains each term: true thinking is seeing things as they are, giving is truly letting go of what was yours. He ranks the eight as a lower discipline and the meditation as the highest; Bhāskara treats the eight as the limbs of the meditation. The anonymous commentator adds that the mind’s one-pointedness is the highest tapas. The record reports these readings and claims nothing about effects.
analogy: Like a coach who lists drills — running, lifting, stretching — and then says that what all of them are for is the game itself.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It calls right, truth, learning, calm, restraint, tranquillity, giving and sacrifice each tapas, and ends: earth, mid-air, heaven — this Brahman is to be meditated on; this is tapas.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa define tapas as the one-pointedness of mind and senses, the means to knowledge, citing a verse they call śruti: «मनसश्चेन्द्रियाणां च ह्यैकाग्र्यं परमं तपः». The anuvāka praises that tapas as present in all the rites of śruti and smṛti, or gives a japa to achieve it.

commentary.q: How do the eight relate to the meditation?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa calls the eight a lower austerity and the meditation the highest: «तदेतत्सर्वमर्वाचीनं तपः» and «तदेतदुपासनमुत्तमं तपः»; the Brahman meditated on is Virāj, the three worlds («भूरादिलोकत्रयात्मकं विराहरूपं यद्ब्रह्मास्ति»). Bhāskara makes the eight the limbs of the meditation and quotes the Taittirīya, ‘seek to know Brahman by tapas; tapas is Brahman’: «तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व । तपो ब्रह्म».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base writes सत्त्यं; the Ānandāśrama text and the Tirupati e-text have सत्यं, and the base’s spacing differs from theirs (listed for review). The Tirupati e-text prints the whole anuvāka a second time with उपास्व for उपास्य; the sources page records it as an addition. The base’s upāsya is kept.

schools.disagreement: The commentaries available are ritual and Vedic; they take no position on which the Vedānta schools named here divide. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here).

parallels.note: The Taittirīya’s Śīkṣāvallī lists right, truth, austerity, restraint and calm, each with study and teaching; this anuvāka lists similar goods and calls each tapas.

contemporary.text: The list takes a word that usually means hardship and attaches it to honesty, learning, generosity and calm. It suggests that the hardest discipline is not pain but steady goodness. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Which item on the list would be the hardest discipline for you, and why?
reflect.deeper: If every virtue is tapas, what makes meditation on Brahman the tapas? Do the commentators answer differently?
reflect.practice: Choose one item — true speech, giving, calm — and practise it deliberately for one day.

flags.note: सत्त्यं (base) against सत्यं (Ānandāśrama, Tirupati), with spacing differences in ऋतं तपस्सत्त्यं: listed on the sources page for checking.
उपास्य (base) against उपास्व (Tirupati’s second copy) and the commentators’ upāssva: the base is kept.
